title: Jellyfish Alternatives – A Comprehensive Comparison
summary: Searching for Jellyfish alternatives? Discover how Waydev gives engineering leaders clearer metrics, fully customizable reports, and reliable insights.
body_markdown:
**Short answer.** Both platforms read the same raw signals from Git and Jira without asking engineers to log anything. Jellyfish is built around engineering investment and financial reporting for the board. Waydev is built around delivery, developer experience and AI impact, with self-hosted deployment and an open API for teams that need the data in their own systems.


If your first question is “what did we spend engineering on last quarter,” Jellyfish answers it well. If it is “where is delivery breaking down, and what is AI actually doing to our throughput and quality,” that is where[Waydev](https://waydev.co/) is built to go deeper.


Waydev is a software engineering intelligence platform for engineering leaders. It connects to your version control and issue tracking systems, then surfaces what you need to improve delivery speed, team health and planning accuracy.[Request a free trial](https://waydev.co/demo/) .

## Where Waydev goes further


**You can run it inside your own perimeter** Waydev offers cloud and on-premise deployment, with self-hosted Git and ticketing integrations on the Enterprise plan. For regulated industries and organizations that will not send commit data to a vendor cloud, this is usually the deciding factor rather than a feature preference.


**The data does not stay locked in the dashboard** An open API pulls data out and pushes data in, so engineering metrics can feed the executive reporting, data warehouse or internal tooling you already run. Over 200 integrations cover the rest of the stack.


**Code quality sits next to delivery data** Waydev pulls Sonar data so quality metrics appear alongside issue tracking and version control. Speed without a quality reading beside it is the most common way a metrics program misleads its owner.


**AI impact, not just AI adoption**[WAY AI agents](https://way.dev/) and the[Waydev AI Copilot](https://waydev.co/waydev-ai-launch) surface where AI tooling is changing throughput, review load and quality, rather than reporting seat counts. Adoption is easy to measure and tells you very little on its own.


**Scale and customization** The platform runs for organizations with more than 10,000 active contributors, with custom metrics, custom dashboards and granular filtering rather than a fixed report set.


**You can try it before you commit** Waydev runs a proof of concept on your own repositories before any purchase, and publishes pricing. Jellyfish requires a sales conversation to see either.


## Where Jellyfish is the better fit


Every honest comparison has this section. Here is ours.


Jellyfish is strong when the primary audience for engineering data is the finance organization and the board. Its investment allocation and software capitalization tooling is mature, it has been recognized as a leader in G2’s software development analytics category for seventeen consecutive quarters, and its executive dashboards are built for exactly that conversation.3


If your top three questions are all about R&D spend classification, capitalization and initiative-level cost reporting, Jellyfish is a reasonable choice. Waydev is the stronger fit when delivery health, developer experience, AI impact and deployment control matter more than accounting output.

## Inside the Waydev platform


Waydev is organized into four modules. Each answers a different question, and they read from the same commit-level source.


### Delivery


Measure, optimize and improve every stage of software delivery.


**[Pull Request Insights](https://waydev.co/pull-request-insights/)** Visualize every PR, find where reviews stall, and isolate the specific roadblocks behind a slow stage.


**[DORA metrics](https://waydev.co/dora-metrics/)** Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore, tracked as a trend rather than a snapshot.


**Cycle time** How quickly work moves from first commit to delivery, broken into coding, review and deployment so you can see which stage is actually costing you.


Cycle time split by stage, which is where the bottleneck usually becomes obvious.


### Health


Team dynamics, working practices and the conditions behind delivery numbers.


**[Developer Experience](https://waydev.co/features/developer-experience-dx/)** The friction your contributors hit day to day, which is the part delivery metrics never explain on their own.


**Team and contributor insights** A summary of recent activity by team and by person, built for understanding load distribution rather than ranking individuals.


**Benchmark and hygiene** How teams compare against company standards, and whether work is being tracked consistently enough for the rest of the data to be trustworthy.


### Planning


Align engineering work with product and business strategy.


**Resource planning** Where engineering capacity is allocated, what it costs, and how key initiatives are progressing against that allocation.


**Project costs** Cost and progress on key initiatives and deliverables, so schedule conversations happen before the slip rather than after it.


### Automation


Targets track key metrics against benchmarks, and notifications fire when a team hits a milestone or a threshold moves the wrong way. The[work log](https://waydev.co/features/work-log/) removes the guesswork about where effort actually went.


## How Jellyfish approaches the same problem


Jellyfish gathers engineering signals from commits and pull requests in Git and from tasks in Jira, then layers contextual data from calendars, product planning tools and HR systems to build a picture of what teams are working on and how long it takes.


The output is oriented toward allocation: work and resources mapped to projects, releases and business objectives. Their main reports cover alignment, investment distribution across roadmap, unplanned, infrastructure and support work, technical debt, product pillars, and productivity. Like Waydev, it requires no manual input from engineers.

## Common questions


### Does Jellyfish offer DORA metrics?


Yes. Jellyfish tracks DORA metrics including lead time, deployment frequency and mean time to resolution.1 DORA coverage alone is not a reason to choose between the two platforms. Deployment model, data portability and depth of developer experience data are.


### Is SOC 3 a higher level of certification than SOC 2?


No, and it is worth stating plainly. A SOC 3 report can only be issued after a clean SOC 2 Type II audit, and it is a public-facing summary of that same examination.4 The practical benefit is that Waydev’s SOC 3 report can be shared freely without an NDA, while a SOC 2 report typically cannot. Both platforms hold SOC 2.


### Can we migrate historical data?


Waydev backfills from your existing version control and issue tracking history, up to 6 months on Pro and 36 months on Premium, so trend analysis starts on day one rather than after a quarter of collection.


### Do engineers have to change how they work?


No, for either platform. Both read signals that your Git provider and issue tracker already produce.


### Which is better for a finance-led reporting requirement?


Jellyfish, if software capitalization and R&D spend classification are the primary use case. Waydev, if delivery performance, developer experience and AI impact carry more weight than accounting output.


## Compare the two on your own data
